lesson.title: SQL Basics
lesson.summary: Select book titles from a supplied table and put the results in order.
explanation: SQL is a language for asking a database questions. A database stores organized data. A table contains rows, one for each thing, and columns, one for each detail. In the exercise, each books row describes one book. Its id identifies it, title stores its name, and status tells whether it has been read. Reading rows with SELECT does not edit those saved books.

Here is a complete separate SQLite example. Run this block once in a fresh database. TEXT stores text; INTEGER stores whole numbers. PRIMARY KEY makes each id identify one row. Parentheses group columns or values; commas separate them; a semicolon finishes each SQL statement. Single quotes mark text values.
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_books (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT,
  status TEXT
);
INSERT INTO demo_books VALUES
  (1, 'Ocean Map', 'unread'),
  (2, 'Apple Tree', 'read'),
  (3, 'Cloud Diary', 'unread');
SELECT title, status
FROM demo_books;
```
The final query returns all three books and both selected columns. INSERT supplies values in the table's column order.

SELECT chooses the columns to return. FROM names the table to read. WHERE tests each row and keeps only rows whose test is true. The equals sign in SQL compares values: status = 'unread' asks whether the status text matches unread. This equals sign does not assign a new status. Capitalized keywords make the query easier to scan; their capitalization does not change its meaning.

Now run this query after the previous setup:
```sql
SELECT title
FROM demo_books
WHERE status = 'unread'
ORDER BY title ASC;
```
FROM reads demo_books; WHERE keeps Ocean Map and Cloud Diary; SELECT returns only their titles. ORDER BY title arranges the returned titles alphabetically. ASC means ascending, and is the default: Cloud Diary appears before Ocean Map. The read book Apple Tree is excluded even though its title would sort first.

Without ORDER BY, the database promises no particular result order. The order may look stable on a small table and change later. DESC requests descending order instead. Sorting changes the order of the answer, not the order in which the books are stored. For numbers, ascending goes from smaller to larger; for these English titles, it goes alphabetically.

For a numeric example, sorting 11, 3, 7 in ascending order produces 3, 7, 11: choose the smallest first, then the next smallest. Sorting text uses text comparison, not numeric arithmetic.

The exercise wants a temporary answer table. CREATE TEMP TABLE answer AS followed by SELECT saves that query's result in a table named answer for this database session. AS here connects the table to the query that fills it. The starter has WHERE 0: zero is false, so it creates an empty answer table. Replace that false condition with the actual status test, and select just title. Saving rows in a table does not give that table an inherent display order. After creating answer, use SELECT title FROM answer ORDER BY title to display it.

Before running your exercise, inspect setup.sql. River Notes and Small Atlas are unread; Moon Garden and Quiet Room are read. Keep only the unread rows. In your final display query, ORDER BY title puts River Notes first. Use single quotes for text values. The checks verify saved result membership, not a table's physical row order; inspect the explicitly ordered display separately.

quiz.question: A SELECT query has no ORDER BY. It appeared alphabetically once. Can the app rely on that order next time?
choices: Yes; the first displayed order becomes permanent
Yes; selecting title always sorts by title
No; add ORDER BY title when that order is required
quiz.explanation: A result without ORDER BY has no promised presentation order. Selecting a column does not request sorting by it.

hints: Open setup.sql and note which books have status unread.
Filter on status="unread".
Sort by title and save the result as answer.

lesson.title: Table Management
lesson.summary: Create a table, add rows, update one row, and remove a selected row.
explanation: SQL can change saved rows as well as read them. CREATE TABLE defines a table's columns. INSERT INTO adds a row; UPDATE changes rows already there; DELETE FROM removes rows. These operations have different jobs. To make an edit safely, first be clear about which row you mean. An id is useful because a primary key identifies one row even when names are repeated.

Run this complete practice setup once in a fresh SQLite database:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_collection (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT,
  count INTEGER CHECK(count >= 0)
);
INSERT INTO demo_collection (id, name, count)
VALUES
  (1, 'Stones', 6),
  (2, 'Tickets', 2),
  (3, 'Ribbons', 4);
SELECT id, name, count
FROM demo_collection
ORDER BY id;
```
The result has three rows. The explicit column list tells SQL which value belongs to which column. CHECK(count >= 0) refuses a row whose count is negative; >= means greater than or equal to.

An INSERT can name its columns and give one new set of VALUES. An UPDATE uses SET to say what changes, then WHERE to choose the existing rows. In SET count = count + 1, the right side reads the old count and adds one; the left side names the column that receives the result. In WHERE id = 1, equals compares the id with 1. Its meaning depends on its place.

Run this after the setup:
```sql
INSERT INTO demo_collection (id, name, count)
VALUES (4, 'Pins', 3);
UPDATE demo_collection
SET count = count + 1
WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE demo_collection
SET name = 'Train tickets'
WHERE id = 2;
DELETE FROM demo_collection
WHERE id = 3;
SELECT name, count
FROM demo_collection
ORDER BY id;
```
You get Stones with 7, Train tickets with 2, and Pins with 3. The first command adds; the next two edit; the fourth removes Ribbons. The last query reads the finished table.

WHERE is especially important for writes. UPDATE without WHERE changes every row; DELETE without WHERE removes every row. A WHERE that matches nothing makes no change, like the starter's id = -1. Before editing, a SELECT with the same WHERE can show which rows will match. A text comparison must match the stored name, including its spaces. Renaming a row also changes which name will match next time.

The exercise already supplies collection, so do not create it again. Add Cards with id 4 and count 1, increase Shells from 3 to 4, rename Badges to Travel badges, and remove Coins. Each edit should have a narrow condition. A final SELECT can help you see the rows, but this exercise checks collection itself; creating a separate answer table does not perform the requested edits.

Check both values and membership: exactly three rows should remain, with no Coins row. Increasing a count should leave the other counts alone. INSERT does not rename an old row, and ORDER BY does not add one. If you rerun an INSERT in the same unchanged database, the repeated primary key can cause an error; use a fresh practice setup when starting this walkthrough again.

Counting uses the same idea of one added item per step. If you record one task each day for seven days, the count is 7 × 1 = 7. Updating a count by one once per day would produce 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

lesson.title: Filters
lesson.summary: Filter a supplied activity table by name and difficulty.
explanation: A filter is a condition that decides which rows belong in a result. WHERE reads a row's details and asks a true-or-false question. You can combine questions: AND requires both to be true; OR requires at least one. Choosing rows with SELECT and WHERE does not delete the rows that fail the filter. They stay in the saved table.

This complete SQLite setup gives us three activities to examine:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_activities (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT,
  difficulty TEXT,
  minutes INTEGER
);
INSERT INTO demo_activities VALUES
  (1, 'Draw a leaf', 'easy', 8),
  (2, 'Build a bridge', 'hard', 8),
  (3, 'Read a chapter', 'easy', 18);
SELECT name, minutes
FROM demo_activities
WHERE minutes <= 8;
```
The query returns Draw a leaf and Build a bridge. <= means less than or equal to: 8 passes, while 18 does not.

The comparison symbols have precise boundaries. < excludes equality; <= includes it. > means greater than; >= includes the equal case. For text, difficulty = 'easy' matches a particular stored value. These two tests describe different details: being easy does not tell us how long an activity takes. We need both tests when both requirements matter.

Run this on the same practice table:
```sql
SELECT name
FROM demo_activities
WHERE difficulty = 'easy'
  AND minutes <= 8
ORDER BY name;
```
Only Draw a leaf appears. Build a bridge passes the time test but fails the difficulty test. Read a chapter passes the difficulty test but fails the time test. AND rejects both. The line break before AND is just formatting; it remains part of the same WHERE condition.

If you used OR instead, all three practice activities would pass because each satisfies at least one condition. Sorting cannot rescue a failed filter: ORDER BY arranges the rows that were kept; it does not make a false condition true. Parentheses help make grouping explicit when a future query combines AND and OR, for example (difficulty = 'easy' OR difficulty = 'medium') AND minutes <= 8.

For the exercise, select name from activities and keep difficulty 'easy' AND minutes at most 10. Ten is included because the symbol is <=. An easy activity taking 25 minutes fails because 25 <= 10 is false. Save the selected names using CREATE TEMP TABLE answer AS followed by your query; replace the starter's WHERE 0, which deliberately matches no rows.

Read the supplied fixture before predicting the result. Tiny quiz takes 5 minutes and Word puzzle takes 10, so both pass. Code maze and Logic grid do not pass the combined tests. ORDER BY name puts Tiny quiz before Word puzzle. Keeping the query column as name matters because the check reads that column from answer. A saved table has no inherent display order. Use SELECT name FROM answer ORDER BY name for display; these checks verify membership rather than table scan order.

analogy.familiar: A search card with two checkboxes
analogy.connection: An activity must be easy and take at most ten minutes.
analogy.limit: Filtering changes returned rows, not stored rows.

steps: Put both filter checks in `WHERE`.
Use `<=` so the time limit itself is allowed.
Connect the checks with `AND` so both must be true.

lesson.title: Aggregate Functions
lesson.summary: Group sessions by subject and calculate counts, totals, and averages.
explanation: An aggregate function combines several values into one result. COUNT counts, SUM adds, and AVG finds the arithmetic average: total divided by the number of known values. GROUP BY makes separate groups before those calculations. A report grouped by subject returns one row for each subject, rather than one row for every session.

Run this complete SQLite example once:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_sessions (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  subject TEXT,
  minutes INTEGER
);
INSERT INTO demo_sessions VALUES
  (1, 'Art', 12),
  (2, 'Art', 24),
  (3, 'Music', 18),
  (4, 'Music', NULL);
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows,
       COUNT(minutes) AS known_minutes
FROM demo_sessions;
```
The result is rows 4 and known_minutes 3. NULL represents an unknown or missing value. It is not zero and is not the text 'NULL'. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(minutes) counts rows with a known minutes value.

A function call puts its input inside parentheses, such as SUM(minutes). AS gives a result column a name, also called an alias. The * in COUNT(*) means count every row; it is not multiplication here. SUM and AVG also ignore NULL inputs. Music's missing duration does not mean a zero-minute session, so it should not pull the known average down.

Run this query after that setup:
```sql
SELECT subject,
       COUNT(minutes) AS session_count,
       SUM(minutes) AS total_minutes,
       AVG(minutes) AS average_minutes
FROM demo_sessions
GROUP BY subject
ORDER BY subject;
```
Art has count 2, total 36, average 18. Music has count 1, total 18, average 18. GROUP BY subject gives each function only the rows for that subject. ORDER BY makes the report's order predictable.

If a group contains only NULL minutes, COUNT(minutes) is 0, while SUM(minutes) and AVG(minutes) are NULL. The average is unknown because there are no known durations to divide by. A grouped query over an empty table returns no groups. A nongrouped COUNT query over an empty table returns 0. Keep these cases distinct instead of inventing a measured zero.

The exercise needs subject and three named calculations: session_count, total_minutes, and average_minutes. Use COUNT(minutes), not COUNT(*), for the requested known-session count. Put all calculations in one SELECT and GROUP BY subject. CREATE TEMP TABLE answer AS saves that grouped result. The starter's numeric zeros are placeholders, not calculated totals.

In the supplied sessions, Math has 20 and 40: two known values, total 60, average 30. Spanish has 30 and NULL, so its known count is 1 and its average is 30. Coding has one known value, 50. Keep the report honest about missing values. A correct total alone does not prove that the count or average is correct.

lesson.title: Joins
lesson.summary: Join two supplied tables and include authors who have no books.
explanation: A join connects related rows from two tables. Each author has one id. A book's author_id points to the id of its author. That relationship lets SQL attach the author's name to each book. Joining does not combine all books into a single text value: one author can appear in several output rows when that author has several books.

AS a and AS b give the tables short names. The dot in a.id means the id column from table a. ON specifies the matching condition: a book belongs to an author when b.author_id equals a.id. REFERENCES documents the relationship in the schema; the ON condition is still needed to tell this query how to join. SQLite enforcement of foreign keys must be enabled separately when you rely on that constraint.

Run this query on the same tables:
```sql
SELECT a.name AS author, b.title
FROM demo_authors AS a
LEFT JOIN demo_books AS b
  ON b.author_id = a.id
ORDER BY a.id, b.title;
```
You get Nora/Garden Gate, Nora/Sea Path, Luis/Sky Notes, and Imani/NULL. LEFT JOIN preserves each left-side author. When there is no matching book, right-side columns are NULL in the result. SQL has not stored an imaginary book for Imani.

The left table matters. Putting books on the left preserves books, not bookless authors. Also, a later WHERE b.title IS NOT NULL removes the unmatched author rows and defeats this goal. Use IS NULL to test missing values; value = NULL does not mean 'is missing' in SQL. COUNT(*) on the joined result counts the unmatched placeholder row too, while COUNT(b.title) counts known titles.

Sets describe distinct members. With A = {red, blue} and B = {blue, green}, blue is the only shared member, so the overlap has size 1. A join is related but can repeat matching rows: it is not automatically a set of distinct names.

On the demo tables above:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS joined_rows, COUNT(b.title) AS known_titles
FROM demo_authors AS a
LEFT JOIN demo_books AS b ON b.author_id = a.id;
```
This returns joined_rows=4 and known_titles=3. COUNT receives either * for rows or an expression whose non-NULL values are counted, and returns an integer. It does not change the tables.

The exercise supplies authors and books. Keep authors on the left, join books.author_id to authors.id, and select authors.name AS author with books.title. Save the query in the temporary answer table. The author alias matters because the checks look for that result column. There is no need to remove duplicate author names: repeated names represent distinct books.

Ari Vale has two matches, Bo Lin has one, and Casey North has none. The LEFT JOIN therefore produces four rows, including Casey North with a NULL title. If you got only three rows, check whether you used INNER JOIN or filtered out NULL. If you got too many, check the ON relationship; matching unrelated ids can pair rows incorrectly.

analogy.connection: Each book’s author_id points to authors.id.
analogy.limit: Missing book columns become NULL; SQL does not invent a book row.

lesson.title: Subqueries
lesson.summary: Find scores above the average for their own subject using a subquery.
explanation: A subquery is a query placed inside another query. It can calculate a number that the outer query uses for comparison. An overall average uses all scores. A group average uses only one subject's scores. For this project, each learner's score must be compared with the average for that same subject.

Run this complete SQLite setup and overall-average query:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_scores (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  learner TEXT,
  subject TEXT,
  score INTEGER
);
INSERT INTO demo_scores VALUES
  (1, 'Nia', 'Art', 50),
  (2, 'Leo', 'Art', 70),
  (3, 'Uma', 'Art', 60),
  (4, 'Nia', 'Music', 100),
  (5, 'Leo', 'Music', 80);
SELECT learner, subject, score
FROM demo_scores
WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM demo_scores);
```
The inner query returns the overall average 72. Only the Music scores 100 and 80 exceed it. Parentheses make the inner query a single value used by the outer > comparison.

A correlated subquery refers to the current row of the outer query. Give the outer and inner tables different aliases so the reference is clear. Outer means the row we are deciding about now; inner means rows being averaged. SQL decides results as if it checked each outer row, though the database may optimize how it does the work.

Run the subject-average version on that setup:
```sql
SELECT outer_score.learner,
       outer_score.subject,
       outer_score.score
FROM demo_scores AS outer_score
WHERE outer_score.score > (
  SELECT AVG(inner_score.score)
  FROM demo_scores AS inner_score
  WHERE inner_score.subject = outer_score.subject
);
```
Art's average is 60, so Leo's 70 passes. Music's average is 90, so Nia's 100 passes. Leo's 80 no longer passes. The two aliases keep the inner subject tied to the outer row's subject.

Strictly above means >, not >=. A score equal to its group average is excluded. Be careful with an unqualified column inside a subquery: SQL searches the inner scope first. If both sides refer to the inner table, a condition can compare that row's subject with itself and average all subjects accidentally. Different aliases and fully qualified columns make this mistake visible.

Your answer should contain learner, subject, and score for qualifying rows, saved using CREATE TEMP TABLE answer AS followed by the correlated SELECT. In the corrected exercise fixture, Math has 70, 90, 80, and Dana's 81. Its average is (70 + 90 + 80 + 81) / 4 = 80.25, so Bo's 90 and Dana's 81 pass. Spanish's average remains (95 + 75) / 2 = 85, so Ari's 95 passes. There are three qualifying rows.

An average of no known scores is NULL. A comparison such as score > NULL is unknown and does not pass WHERE. The supplied fixture has known scores in both subjects. To tell whether your query really uses subject averages, try a separate fixture like the walkthrough, where the overall average and group averages choose different rows. Matching one small fixture alone can hide a correlation mistake.

analogy.familiar: A score card compared with its group average
analogy.connection: Compare each learner with others in the same subject.
analogy.limit: Without the subject correlation, the average would mix both subjects.

steps: Name the outer table `outer_scores`.
Name the table in the inner query `inner_scores`.
Calculate the average for rows where the two subject names match.
Keep only outer scores above that subject’s average.
Store the kept rows in `answer`.

lesson.solution:
CREATE TEMP TABLE answer AS
SELECT outer_scores.learner, outer_scores.subject, outer_scores.score
FROM scores AS outer_scores
WHERE outer_scores.score > (
  SELECT AVG(inner_scores.score)
  FROM scores AS inner_scores
  WHERE inner_scores.subject = outer_scores.subject
);

lesson.title: Window functions
lesson.summary: Calculate running totals and ranks within groups using a fixed dataset.
explanation: A window function calculates across related rows while keeping each original row in the result. GROUP BY usually reduces a group to one report row; a window can attach a running total or rank to every practice row. OVER introduces the window's rules: which group to use, which order to follow, and which rows count for a calculation.

Run this complete SQLite setup and running-total query:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_practice (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  subject TEXT,
  day TEXT,
  minutes INTEGER
);
INSERT INTO demo_practice VALUES
  (1, 'Art', '2026-01-01', 10),
  (2, 'Art', '2026-01-02', 25),
  (3, 'Art', '2026-01-03', 25),
  (4, 'Music', '2026-01-01', 8);
SELECT subject, day, minutes,
  SUM(minutes) OVER (
    PARTITION BY subject
    ORDER BY day, id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_total
FROM demo_practice
ORDER BY subject, day, id;
```
Art's totals are 10, 35, 60. Music begins its own total at 8. There are still four output rows.

PARTITION BY subject separates the calculations by subject. ORDER BY day, id inside OVER sets the order for accumulation. Fixed year-month-day text sorts these dates chronologically. id breaks a tie when two sessions share a day. ROWS selects individual rows; UNBOUNDED PRECEDING means the start of the partition, and CURRENT ROW means the row being calculated. SUM adds that whole frame.

Run this ranking query after the same setup:
```sql
SELECT subject, day, minutes,
  RANK() OVER (
    PARTITION BY subject
    ORDER BY minutes DESC
  ) AS duration_rank
FROM demo_practice
ORDER BY subject, day, id;
```
Both Art rows with 25 minutes get rank 1, and the 10-minute row gets rank 3. RANK leaves a gap after a tie because two rows occupy the first two positions. Music's single row ranks 1. Empty parentheses mean RANK needs no direct input argument.

Each window has its own order. Running totals need chronological order; duration ranks need minutes descending, largest first. Do not add id to the ranking order if equal durations should tie: that extra detail would separate them. The outer ORDER BY controls display order, independently of the two window calculations. A rank of 1 does not move that row to the first displayed row by itself.

Mean is another name for the arithmetic average. For 3, 6, 9, add 3 + 6 + 9 = 18, then divide by their count 3: 18 / 3 = 6. A running total stops at each current row; a mean also needs a denominator, so it is a different calculation.

For the exercise, select subject, day, and minutes, then add running_total and duration_rank as named result columns. Save that SELECT as answer. The running-total frame must stop at the current row, rather than sum the entire partition every time. RANK needs PARTITION BY subject so a Spanish session is compared with Spanish sessions.

The supplied Math durations are 20, 30, 30: chronological running totals 20, 50, 80. The two 30-minute entries tie at duration rank 1. Spanish starts again at 15 and then totals 40. The checks now compare every fixture row's running total and rank, including both partitions. They test these results, not every possible input or one required SQL spelling.

lesson.title: Query plans and indexes
lesson.summary: Compare query plans before and after adding an appropriate index.
explanation: An index is an extra structure the database maintains to help it find rows. Think of an index in a book: it can guide you to a topic without reading every page. SQL still decides which rows belong in the result. An index should preserve those intended results; it does not remove duplicates or make every query faster.

Here is a complete small SQLite dataset:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_books (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT,
  genre TEXT
);
INSERT INTO demo_books VALUES
  (1, 'Stone Cities', 'history'),
  (2, 'Cloud Tales', 'fiction'),
  (3, 'Ancient Roads', 'history'),
  (4, 'Trade Routes', 'history');
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT title
FROM demo_books
WHERE genre = 'history'
ORDER BY title
LIMIT 2;
```
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN reports how SQLite plans to find the result; it does not return the titles themselves. The exact plan text can vary. Without a helpful index it may scan rows and use temporary sorting work.

A scan examines many rows. An indexed search can use indexed keys to narrow the search. A composite index has more than one column in a chosen order. An index on genre, title first groups entries by genre, then orders titles within each genre. That fits a query that fixes one genre and sorts by title. LIMIT 2 asks for at most two returned rows.

Run this after the setup:
```sql
CREATE INDEX demo_genre_title
ON demo_books (genre, title);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT title
FROM demo_books
WHERE genre = 'history'
ORDER BY title
LIMIT 2;
SELECT title
FROM demo_books
WHERE genre = 'history'
ORDER BY title
LIMIT 2;
```
The title result is Ancient Roads, then Stone Cities. The new plan may mention the named index. CREATE INDEX builds it; ON names the table and indexed columns. The query's requested rows remain the same.

An index costs storage and work during INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE because its entries must stay current. SQLite chooses a plan; a tiny table may be fast even without an index. Timing depends on machine load, database size, and caching. Compare identical queries and verify identical results before calling an index helpful. A plan is evidence about strategy, not a guarantee of a particular duration.

A full scan that checks each of n rows once has linear work, written O(n). If a 12-row table needs 12 comparisons, a similar 24-row full scan needs about 24: twice the input gives twice the comparisons. This describes growth of work, not a guaranteed elapsed time. An index may avoid that full scan for a suitable query.

The exercise fixture creates 1,000 books with a recursive number generator. WITH RECURSIVE names an intermediate numbers sequence; UNION ALL appends the next values until value < 1000 becomes false. The || operator joins text, forming titles such as Book 10. The % operator finds the remainder: value % 5 = 0 marks every fifth book history. CASE WHEN chooses history for that condition, otherwise fiction. These are setup mechanics; your task is to add the index and query.

Create the specifically named idx_books_genre_title on books(genre, title), then save the first five history titles in answer with ORDER BY title LIMIT 5. Titles sort as text: Book 100 appears before Book 20. The checks compare the index's key-column metadata and exact selected title membership. Display answer with an explicit ORDER BY title. Inspect the demonstrated EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN before and after; neither these checks nor a particular plan proves a speed gain.

lesson.title: Transactions and consistency
lesson.summary: Move a quantity between records atomically and handle a deliberate failure.
explanation: A transaction groups related database changes into one unit. BEGIN starts the unit; COMMIT saves it; ROLLBACK discards its uncommitted changes. A transfer should subtract from one record and add the same quantity to another, so their total stays unchanged. Atomic means the intended changes succeed together or the earlier state is preserved.

The first UPDATE must match both the source id and sufficient stock. SQLite's changes() reports the row count changed by the most recently completed write. Immediately after that source UPDATE, changes() = 1 means one source row changed. The destination UPDATE uses that fact as its guard. Keep the two writes adjacent: an intervening write could change what changes() reports. This pattern assumes the supplied destination exists and the source key identifies one row.

A SQL error does not always roll back an entire SQLite transaction automatically. Real transfer code must handle errors and issue ROLLBACK when needed. It must also verify the destination write; if that destination did not exist, guarding only the source would be insufficient. The exercise's fixed fixture provides both rows. Its deliberate failure is insufficient stock, handled by making both updates no-ops rather than by throwing an error.

In the exercise, transfer 3 from A's 10 to B's 4 inside a transaction. Require quantity >= 3 on the source and changes() = 1 on the immediately following destination update. Commit the valid transfer. Then CREATE TEMP TABLE before_failed AS SELECT id, quantity FROM inventory records the finished state for comparison. A snapshot here is a copied set of values, not another transfer.

Try the 99-unit attempt using the same guards. A has only 7, so the source changes zero rows; changes() is 0, so the destination also changes zero. COMMIT then saves no changes. Both stay at 7, their total remains 14, and the snapshot still matches. Conservation alone would not catch every incorrect distribution; check both individual quantities and unchanged state after rejection.

lesson.title: A supply category directory
lesson.summary: Create a view named category_directory with one column, category. Read supplies, omit NULL and empty-string categories, and keep each remaining category once. Display the view sorted by category. Keep spaces and capitalization as stored; the supplied categories need no cleanup.
explanation: A directory should list each category once even when many supplies belong to it. A SQL table stores rows under named columns. SELECT chooses columns; FROM chooses a table. DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows. This lesson builds a reusable directory from the supplies table rather than manually typing the category names.

SELECT DISTINCT category returns each different category value once. DISTINCT applies to the whole selected row. If you also select item_name, two rows with the same category and different items remain different rows. Choose only the column that defines the directory entry.

This self-contained example uses a temporary set of values.
```sql
WITH supplies(category) AS (
  VALUES ('paper'), ('tools'), ('paper')
)
SELECT DISTINCT category
FROM supplies
ORDER BY category;
```
The result has paper and tools once each. WITH gives this query a named input; it does not create a permanent table.

NULL represents missing information. It differs from the empty string, which is present text of length zero. Use category IS NOT NULL to omit missing values and category <> '' to omit empty text. The AND keyword requires both conditions to hold. Neither condition trims spaces or changes spelling.

A filter can run before duplicate removal.
```sql
WITH labels(name) AS (VALUES ('A'), (NULL), (''), ('A'), ('B'))
SELECT DISTINCT name
FROM labels
WHERE name IS NOT NULL AND name <> ''
ORDER BY name;
```
The result is A and B. ORDER BY requests output order explicitly; SQL does not promise a useful row order when it is omitted.

A view is a saved query, not a separate copy of its results. CREATE VIEW category_directory AS followed by SELECT defines the reusable query. Later, SELECT * FROM category_directory ORDER BY category displays it. If a new category is added to supplies, the view reads the new data without rebuilding a manual list.

The setup file creates supplies for each run. Your query should create the view without changing those source rows, then display the sorted directory. Checks look for duplicates and omitted empty values in the supplied data. After passing, add a new category in setup.sql and rerun: a real view derives its results from the source instead of storing a manually typed list.

lesson.title: A reachable contact list
lesson.summary: Create a view contact_choices with id, name and contact for every row in contacts. Prefer a nonempty trimmed email, then a nonempty trimmed phone, otherwise use "No contact yet". The stored values can be NULL, empty, or contain outside spaces. Do not change the source table.
explanation: A contact record may be missing an email, a phone number or both. NULL means a missing or unknown value in SQL. An empty string and spaces-only text are present strings, so they need cleanup before a fallback can treat them as missing. This project makes one useful display value per person.

TRIM(text) removes outside spaces in SQLite. It preserves spaces inside a phone number. TRIM(NULL) remains NULL. NULLIF(value, '') returns NULL when value is an empty string and otherwise returns value. Combining them turns an empty or spaces-only field into NULL.

This example shows the cleanup step.
```sql
WITH data(email) AS (VALUES ('  a@example.org  '), (''), ('   '), (NULL))
SELECT NULLIF(TRIM(email), '') AS cleaned
FROM data;
```
The first result is a@example.org. The remaining values are NULL. AS cleaned gives the output column a useful name.

COALESCE chooses the first argument that is not NULL. Its argument order expresses your preference: cleaned email first, cleaned phone second, a written fallback last. COALESCE does not consider a plain empty string missing; that is why the NULLIF cleanup matters.

Here is a complete fallback example.
```sql
WITH people(email, phone) AS (VALUES ('   ', ' 555 0100 '))
SELECT COALESCE(
  NULLIF(TRIM(email), ''),
  NULLIF(TRIM(phone), ''),
  'No contact yet'
) AS contact
FROM people;
```
It returns 555 0100. The outside spaces disappear but the internal space remains.

This is a display choice, not proof that an email or phone number is valid or reachable. Do not invent stricter validation than the task requests. Keep id and name in the view so a caller can associate the chosen contact with the right person. Every input person should produce one output row.

Create the contact_choices view and display it ordered by id. Check a person with both fields, phone only, neither field and spaces-only email. The preference rule must keep email when both are available. The source table should remain unchanged because formatting a view need not edit saved contact details.

analogy.connection: The ordered fallbacks try email, then phone, then a clear missing-contact message.
analogy.limit: A nonempty value can still be mistyped; choosing it does not verify that it works.

lesson.title: An order status dashboard
lesson.summary: Create a view customer_orders with customer_id, name, total_orders, paid_orders and paid_cents. Include every customer, even those without orders. Count all their orders, count only status="paid" orders, and sum only paid amounts. Missing totals must be zero. Amounts are nonnegative integer cents.
explanation: A dashboard may need several summaries from the same data. Aggregation combines rows, using functions such as COUNT and SUM. Conditional aggregation adds a decision inside the aggregate so different summary columns can include different rows. Here, a customer can have paid, pending or cancelled orders.

Start from customers and LEFT JOIN orders using the customer ID. A left join keeps a customer even when no order matches. The unmatched order columns become NULL. COUNT(*) would count that retained row as one, so use COUNT(o.id) to count only real orders; COUNT(column) skips NULL.

CASE turns a condition into a value before SUM adds it.
```sql
WITH orders(status, cents) AS (VALUES ('paid', 300), ('pending', 500), ('paid', 200))
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN cents ELSE 0 END) AS paid_cents
FROM orders;
```
This returns 2 paid orders and 500 paid cents. The pending amount is deliberately excluded.

GROUP BY chooses which rows belong to each summary. Group by customer ID and name. Names alone are unsafe because two different customers can share a name. Aliases such as c for customers and o for orders shorten qualified column names, including c.id and o.customer_id.

This example keeps a customer with no order.
```sql
WITH customers(id) AS (VALUES (1), (2)),
orders(id, customer_id) AS (VALUES (10, 1))
SELECT c.id, COUNT(o.id) AS total_orders
FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id
ORDER BY c.id;
```
Customer 1 has one order; customer 2 has zero. An inner join would lose customer 2 entirely.

Do not place WHERE o.status = 'paid' after the join: it would remove unpaid orders before total_orders is counted and remove customers without paid orders. Put that condition inside each paid aggregate. CASE with ELSE 0 gives the retained no-order row a zero contribution.

Integer cents avoid floating-point rounding for this small monetary total. The view summarizes orders; it does not charge anyone or infer payment from an amount. Checks include two customers sharing a name, a customer with no orders and unpaid orders that must not count toward revenue. Display the final view ordered by customer_id.

analogy.familiar: One summary line for each customer on a shop report
analogy.connection: Conditional totals count different kinds of orders without losing the customer.
analogy.limit: A summary depends on the stored status; it does not verify that a real payment occurred.

steps: Use `LEFT JOIN` to match customers to orders by customer ID.
Count `o.id` to count the orders.
Use one `CASE` expression to count paid orders.
Use another `CASE` expression to add paid amounts.
Group the results by customer ID and name.
Display the view.
lesson.solution:
CREATE VIEW customer_orders AS
SELECT c.id AS customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS total_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN o.amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS paid_cents
FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
SELECT * FROM customer_orders ORDER BY customer_id;

checks.label: A customer with no orders stays with zero totals

checks.label: Matching names remain separate and unpaid orders stay unpaid

lesson.title: A folder path explorer
lesson.summary: Create a view folder_paths with id, path and depth from folders(id, name, parent_id). Roots have NULL parent_id, path equal to their name and depth 0. Children append "/" plus their name and increase depth by 1. Include every folder in the supplied acyclic forest. Names contain no slash; keep the source unchanged.
explanation: A folder tree stores one row per folder and the ID of its parent. A root has no parent. A forest is a collection of separate trees, so there can be several roots. A recursive query repeatedly uses earlier results to find the next level. It can build full paths even when the depth varies.

A common table expression, or CTE, gives a query a temporary name after WITH. WITH RECURSIVE allows a CTE to refer to itself. It has an anchor query that provides starting rows and a recursive query that expands from them. UNION ALL combines the starting and later rows without removing duplicates.

This complete recursive example counts upward.
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (
  SELECT 0
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 3
)
SELECT n FROM numbers ORDER BY n;
```
It produces 0, 1, 2 and 3. The WHERE condition prevents further expansion after 3. A recursive query needs a reason to stop.

For folder paths, the anchor selects rows whose parent_id IS NULL. Give each root its own name as the path and zero as the depth. The recursive part joins a child folder to an already discovered parent path using child.parent_id = parent.id. When no undiscovered descendants remain to expand, the supplied acyclic tree is finished.

SQLite joins text with ||. Here is a small one-level example.
```sql
WITH parent(id, path, depth) AS (VALUES (1, 'Home', 0)),
child(id, name, parent_id) AS (VALUES (2, 'Notes', 1))
SELECT child.id, parent.path || '/' || child.name AS path, parent.depth + 1 AS depth
FROM child JOIN parent ON child.parent_id = parent.id;
```
The output is ID 2, Home/Notes and depth 1. The full recursive query repeats that same expansion at every level.

The input contract guarantees an acyclic forest and existing parents. General untrusted graphs need cycle detection or another explicit bound; this exercise does not claim to handle arbitrary cycles. lesson.title: A folder path explorer
lesson.summary: Create a view folder_paths with id, path and depth from folders(id, name, parent_id). Roots have NULL parent_id, path equal to their name and depth 0. Children append "/" plus their name and increase depth by 1. Include every folder in the supplied acyclic forest. Names contain no slash; keep the source unchanged.
explanation: A folder tree stores one row per folder and the ID of its parent. A root has no parent. A forest is a collection of separate trees, so there can be several roots. A recursive query repeatedly uses earlier results to find the next level. It can build full paths even when the depth varies.

A common table expression, or CTE, gives a query a temporary name after WITH. WITH RECURSIVE allows a CTE to refer to itself. It has an anchor query that provides starting rows and a recursive query that expands from them. UNION ALL combines the starting and later rows without removing duplicates.

This complete recursive example counts upward.
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (
  SELECT 0
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 3
)
SELECT n FROM numbers ORDER BY n;
```
It produces 0, 1, 2 and 3. The WHERE condition prevents further expansion after 3. A recursive query needs a reason to stop.

For folder paths, the anchor selects rows whose parent_id IS NULL. Give each root its own name as the path and zero as the depth. The recursive part joins a child folder to an already discovered parent path using child.parent_id = parent.id. When no undiscovered descendants remain to expand, the supplied acyclic tree is finished.

SQLite joins text with ||. Here is a small one-level example.

WITH parent(id, path, depth) AS (VALUES (1, 'Home', 0)),
child(id, name, parent_id) AS (VALUES (2, 'Notes', 1))
SELECT child.id, parent.path || '/' || child.name AS path, parent.depth + 1 AS depth
FROM child JOIN parent ON child.parent_id = parent.id;
```
The output is ID 2, Home/Notes and depth 1. The full recursive query repeats that same expansion at every level.

lesson.title: Keep subjects that meet the total
lesson.summary: Create a view named qualifying_subjects with subject and total_minutes. Include subjects whose summed known minutes are at least 30. Display the result ordered by subject. Do not modify sessions.
explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before they are grouped.
GROUP BY puts rows with the same group value together. SUM then adds the known numbers in each group.
HAVING filters the grouped results. It can ask a question about SUM(minutes).

This separate example keeps a group whose total reaches 20.
```sql
WITH practice(subject, minutes) AS (
  VALUES ('Drawing', 8), ('Drawing', 14), ('Singing', 15)
)
SELECT subject, SUM(minutes) AS total_minutes
FROM practice
GROUP BY subject
HAVING SUM(minutes) >= 20
ORDER BY subject;
```
Drawing remains with 22 minutes. Neither individual Drawing row reaches 20, but the total does.
Using WHERE minutes >= 20 instead would remove both Drawing rows before addition. It answers a different question.
The >= comparison includes the exact boundary. A total of 30 qualifies when the minimum is 30.
SUM ignores NULL inputs. A group with only NULL minutes has an unknown total, so it does not pass this numeric condition.
Create the view from a grouped SELECT. A view saves the query; it is not a separate copied table.
Check a group that reaches the target through several small entries, one just below the target, and one with unknown minutes.

lesson.title: Keep every note attached to an author
lesson.summary: Enable foreign keys and create notes with id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, author_id INTEGER NOT NULL referencing authors(id), and title TEXT NOT NULL. Insert note 1 for author 2 with title Moon. Do not change authors.
explanation: A constraint is a rule the database checks when data changes.
NOT NULL rejects a missing value in that column. It does not reject an empty string by itself.
A foreign key links a stored value to a key in another table. It can stop a note from naming an author who does not exist.

SQLite requires foreign-key enforcement to be enabled on the connection. Do this before beginning a transaction.
```sql
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
```
With enforcement on, a player cannot refer to team 8 unless teams already has id 8.
An ordinary join reads relationships; it does not enforce them. The foreign-key constraint checks future writes.
In the practice, authors already contains ids 1 and 2. Create notes, then store the note belonging to author 2.

An attempt to use author 99 should fail instead of creating an orphan note. A missing author_id should fail because NOT NULL is also required. The project checks inspect connection/schema metadata and the accepted row. They do not execute expected failing writes as learner checks. The separate local constraint demonstrations in the later row-rule and relationship lessons show those errors; do not insert a deliberate failure into this normal solution.

lesson.title: Make one invitation list
lesson.summary: Create a view invitations with one name column combining names in morning and afternoon, with each distinct name once. Display it alphabetically. Preserve both source tables.
explanation: UNION combines the rows produced by two SELECT queries.
Both queries must return the same number of columns. Here each returns a single name column.

UNION removes duplicate result rows.
```sql
SELECT 'Ari' AS name
UNION
SELECT 'Ari' AS name;
```
This returns one Ari row, not two.

UNION ALL keeps every result row, including repeated ones.
```sql
SELECT 'Ari' AS name
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Ari' AS name;
```
This returns two Ari rows. Keeping duplicates is useful when each occurrence represents a separate event.
Use UNION for one invitation per distinct name in this simplified exercise. In a real contact system, names alone are not reliable unique person identifiers.
ORDER BY at the end sorts the combined result. It does not decide which duplicates are removed.
A view can save the combined SELECT for reuse. The source rows remain in their original tables.

lesson.title: Find customers who have paid orders
lesson.summary: Create a view paid_customers(id,name) containing each customer with at least one paid order. Multiple paid orders must not duplicate that customer. Keep source tables unchanged.
explanation:
EXISTS asks whether a subquery returns at least one row.

The supplied practice database contains customers(id, name) and orders(id, customer_id, status). The names inside parentheses are the available columns; use these exact identifiers when reading the fixture tables.
It is a yes-or-no condition. It does not add all matching child rows to the outer result.

A correlated subquery refers to the current outer row. Run this complete example in a fresh database.
```sql
CREATE TABLE authors(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE books(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,author_id INTEGER);
INSERT INTO authors VALUES(1),(2);
INSERT INTO books VALUES(10,1),(11,1);
SELECT a.id
FROM authors AS a
WHERE EXISTS(
SELECT 1
FROM books AS b
WHERE b.author_id=a.id)
ORDER BY a.id;
SELECT a.id
FROM authors AS a
WHERE NOT EXISTS(
SELECT 1
FROM books AS b
WHERE b.author_id=a.id)
ORDER BY a.id;
```
The first result contains ID 1 once, despite two matching books. The NOT EXISTS result contains ID 2.
For each author, the inner query asks whether any matching book exists. SELECT 1 is enough because the condition needs existence, not a book’s data.
Keep the relationship condition inside the subquery. Without b.author_id = a.id, any book could make every author qualify.
For your practice, require both the matching customer ID and status equal to paid.
A customer with no paid orders is excluded even if they have pending orders. A customer with several paid orders appears only once.
NOT EXISTS would ask the opposite question: no matching row. It differs from assuming every customer without a match has a zero-valued order.

lesson.title: Summarize paid work in two readable steps
lesson.summary: Create a view paid_totals(customer_id,total) summing paid order amounts by customer. Use an ordinary CTE named paid to first select paid orders. Keep only totals at least 10. Do not change orders.
explanation:
An ordinary common table expression gives a query result a temporary name within one statement.

The supplied practice database contains orders(customer_id, status, amount). The names inside parentheses are the available columns; use these exact identifiers when reading the fixture tables.
WITH introduces that name before the main query. Unlike a saved view, the name does not remain available to later statements.

This complete example names a filtered result before summing it. The first named row set supplies the input values.
```sql
WITH demo(amount) AS(VALUES(-2),(3),(4)),
positive AS(
SELECT amount
FROM demo
WHERE amount>0)
SELECT SUM(amount) AS total
FROM positive;
```
The total is 7: only 3 and 4 contribute.
The name positive refers to the query result, not a separately stored table.
Breaking a complex query into named steps can make its intent easier to inspect. It does not automatically make it faster.
For this practice, paid selects the customer_id and amount of paid orders. The outer query groups that result and filters its totals.
HAVING applies the minimum to the group total. Applying the minimum to each original amount would discard small orders that should contribute.
CREATE VIEW can wrap the complete WITH statement so the final report has a reusable name.

lesson.title: Update an existing preference without duplicating it
lesson.summary: Store theme=dark and language=en in settings. Existing theme must be updated, missing language inserted, and the unrelated font preference preserved. Use the key uniqueness constraint to handle conflicts.
explanation: An INSERT can conflict with a UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint when its key already exists.
UPSERT describes what to do for that uniqueness conflict: update the matching row or leave it unchanged.
excluded.value refers to the value the attempted insertion would have stored.
The conflict target key chooses the uniqueness rule being handled. It does not mean every kind of constraint failure should be ignored.
Updating an existing row is different from adding a duplicate preference. The primary key ensures there is only one row per key.
For the practice, apply the same insert-or-update behavior to theme and language. Do not clear the settings table.
Check an existing key, a missing key, and an unrelated key that must survive unchanged.

lesson.title: Undo a trial change but keep the approved change
lesson.summary: Begin a transaction. Increase account 1 balance from 10 to 15, then create savepoint trial. Temporarily set account 2 balance to 99, roll back only to trial, release it, and commit. Final balances must be 15 and 20.
explanation: A transaction can contain a named savepoint for a smaller reversible portion of its work.
ROLLBACK TO returns to the state at that savepoint without cancelling the whole outer transaction.
Changes made before the savepoint remain part of the transaction.
ROLLBACK TO does not itself remove the named savepoint. RELEASE removes that mark after you are finished with it.
Releasing an inner savepoint is not the same as committing the outer transaction. A later outer rollback can still undo its changes.
In this practice, the first account changes before trial. Only the second account’s tentative update should be undone.
Use this only on the supplied isolated data. It is a transaction lesson, not a real financial operation.

lesson.title: Record only real title changes
lesson.summary: Create an AFTER UPDATE OF title trigger named record_title_change on notes. When the new title differs from the old title, insert note ID, old title, and new title into note_audit. Then run the supplied updates; an unchanged title must not create an audit row.
explanation: A trigger is database work that runs automatically when its specified event happens. Unlike a SELECT, it can cause additional writes.
The supplied database has notes(id,title) and note_audit(note_id,old_title,new_title). Titles are never NULL in this fixture.
In an UPDATE trigger, OLD refers to the row before the update and NEW refers to the row after it. OLD.title and NEW.title read those two title values.
AFTER means the row update happens before this trigger’s work. UPDATE OF title identifies updates assigning that column, even when the assigned value equals the old value.
WHEN NEW.title <> OLD.title limits the trigger to changed titles. The <> operator means not equal. Use NEW.id for the note identity.
The supplied operations change note 1 from Moon to Moon draft, leave note 2 at Sea, then change note 1 to Moon final. The audit should contain exactly the two actual changes, in their recorded order.
Use the isolated practice data only. Triggers run inside database operations and their effects participate in transactions; test them before applying them to real stored data.

lesson.title: SQL Basics
lesson.summary: Select book titles from a supplied table and put the results in order.
explanation: SQL is a language for asking a database questions. A database stores organized data. A table contains rows, one for each thing, and columns, one for each detail. In the exercise, each books row describes one book. Its id identifies it, title stores its name, and status tells whether it has been read. Reading rows with SELECT does not edit those saved books.

Here is a complete separate SQLite example. Run this block once in a fresh database. TEXT stores text; INTEGER stores whole numbers. PRIMARY KEY makes each id identify one row. Parentheses group columns or values; commas separate them; a semicolon finishes each SQL statement. Single quotes mark text values.
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_books (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT,
  status TEXT
);
INSERT INTO demo_books VALUES
  (1, 'Ocean Map', 'unread'),
  (2, 'Apple Tree', 'read'),
  (3, 'Cloud Diary', 'unread');
SELECT title, status
FROM demo_books;
```
The final query returns all three books and both selected columns. INSERT supplies values in the table's column order.

SELECT chooses the columns to return. FROM names the table to read. WHERE tests each row and keeps only rows whose test is true. The equals sign in SQL compares values: status = 'unread' asks whether the status text matches unread. This equals sign does not assign a new status. Capitalized keywords make the query easier to scan; their capitalization does not change its meaning.

Now run this query after the previous setup:
```sql
SELECT title
FROM demo_books
WHERE status = 'unread'
ORDER BY title ASC;
```
FROM reads demo_books; WHERE keeps Ocean Map and Cloud Diary; SELECT returns only their titles. ORDER BY title arranges the returned titles alphabetically. ASC means ascending, and is the default: Cloud Diary appears before Ocean Map. The read book Apple Tree is excluded even though its title would sort first.

Without ORDER BY, the database promises no particular result order. The order may look stable on a small table and change later. DESC requests descending order instead. Sorting changes the order of the answer, not the order in which the books are stored. For numbers, ascending goes from smaller to larger; for these English titles, it goes alphabetically.

For a numeric example, sorting 11, 3, 7 in ascending order produces 3, 7, 11: choose the smallest first, then the next smallest. Sorting text uses text comparison, not numeric arithmetic.

The exercise wants a temporary answer table. CREATE TEMP TABLE answer AS followed by SELECT saves that query's result in a table named answer for this database session. AS here connects the table to the query that fills it. The starter has WHERE 0: zero is false, so it creates an empty answer table. Replace that false condition with the actual status test, and select just title. Saving rows in a table does not give that table an inherent display order. After creating answer, use SELECT title FROM answer ORDER BY title to display it.

Before running your exercise, inspect setup.sql. River Notes and Small Atlas are unread; Moon Garden and Quiet Room are read. Keep only the unread rows. In your final display query, ORDER BY title puts River Notes first. Use single quotes for text values. The checks verify saved result membership, not a table's physical row order; inspect the explicitly ordered display separately.

lesson.title: Table Management
lesson.summary: Create a table, add rows, update one row, and remove a selected row.
explanation: SQL can change saved rows as well as read them. CREATE TABLE defines a table's columns. INSERT INTO adds a row; UPDATE changes rows already there; DELETE FROM removes rows. These operations have different jobs. To make an edit safely, first be clear about which row you mean. An id is useful because a primary key identifies one row even when names are repeated.

Run this complete practice setup once in a fresh SQLite database:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_collection (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT,
  count INTEGER CHECK(count >= 0)
);
INSERT INTO demo_collection (id, name, count)
VALUES
  (1, 'Stones', 6),
  (2, 'Tickets', 2),
  (3, 'Ribbons', 4);
SELECT id, name, count
FROM demo_collection
ORDER BY id;
```
The result has three rows. The explicit column list tells SQL which value belongs to which column. CHECK(count >= 0) refuses a row whose count is negative; >= means greater than or equal to.

An INSERT can name its columns and give one new set of VALUES. An UPDATE uses SET to say what changes, then WHERE to choose the existing rows. In SET count = count + 1, the right side reads the old count and adds one; the left side names the column that receives the result. In WHERE id = 1, equals compares the id with 1. Its meaning depends on its place.

Run this after the setup:
```sql
INSERT INTO demo_collection (id, name, count)
VALUES (4, 'Pins', 3);
UPDATE demo_collection
SET count = count + 1
WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE demo_collection
SET name = 'Train tickets'
WHERE id = 2;
DELETE FROM demo_collection
WHERE id = 3;
SELECT name, count
FROM demo_collection
ORDER BY id;
```
You get Stones with 7, Train tickets with 2, and Pins with 3. The first command adds; the next two edit; the fourth removes Ribbons. The last query reads the finished table.

WHERE is especially important for writes. UPDATE without WHERE changes every row; DELETE without WHERE removes every row. A WHERE that matches nothing makes no change, like the starter's id = -1. Before editing, a SELECT with the same WHERE can show which rows will match. A text comparison must match the stored name, including its spaces. Renaming a row also changes which name will match next time.

The exercise already supplies collection, so do not create it again. Add Cards with id 4 and count 1, increase Shells from 3 to 4, rename Badges to Travel badges, and remove Coins. Each edit should have a narrow condition. A final SELECT can help you see the rows, but this exercise checks collection itself; creating a separate answer table does not perform the requested edits.

Check both values and membership: exactly three rows should remain, with no Coins row. Increasing a count should leave the other counts alone. INSERT does not rename an old row, and ORDER BY does not add one. If you rerun an INSERT in the same unchanged database, the repeated primary key can cause an error; use a fresh practice setup when starting this walkthrough again.

Counting uses the same idea of one added item per step. If you record one task each day for seven days, the count is 7 × 1 = 7. Updating a count by one once per day would produce 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.

lesson.title: Filters
lesson.summary: Filter a supplied activity table by name and difficulty.
explanation: A filter is a condition that decides which rows belong in a result. WHERE reads a row's details and asks a true-or-false question. You can combine questions: AND requires both to be true; OR requires at least one. Choosing rows with SELECT and WHERE does not delete the rows that fail the filter. They stay in the saved table.

This complete SQLite setup gives us three activities to examine:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_activities (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT,
  difficulty TEXT,
  minutes INTEGER
);
INSERT INTO demo_activities VALUES
  (1, 'Draw a leaf', 'easy', 8),
  (2, 'Build a bridge', 'hard', 8),
  (3, 'Read a chapter', 'easy', 18);
SELECT name, minutes
FROM demo_activities
WHERE minutes <= 8;
```
The query returns Draw a leaf and Build a bridge. <= means less than or equal to: 8 passes, while 18 does not.

The comparison symbols have precise boundaries. < excludes equality; <= includes it. > means greater than; >= includes the equal case. For text, difficulty = 'easy' matches a particular stored value. These two tests describe different details: being easy does not tell us how long an activity takes. We need both tests when both requirements matter.

Run this on the same practice table:
```sql
SELECT name
FROM demo_activities
WHERE difficulty = 'easy'
  AND minutes <= 8
ORDER BY name;
```
Only Draw a leaf appears. Build a bridge passes the time test but fails the difficulty test. Read a chapter passes the difficulty test but fails the time test. AND rejects both. The line break before AND is just formatting; it remains part of the same WHERE condition.

If you used OR instead, all three practice activities would pass because each satisfies at least one condition. Sorting cannot rescue a failed filter: ORDER BY arranges the rows that were kept; it does not make a false condition true. Parentheses help make grouping explicit when a future query combines AND and OR, for example (difficulty = 'easy' OR difficulty = 'medium') AND minutes <= 8.

For the exercise, select name from activities and keep difficulty 'easy' AND minutes at most 10. Ten is included because the symbol is <=. An easy activity taking 25 minutes fails because 25 <= 10 is false. Save the selected names using CREATE TEMP TABLE answer AS followed by your query; replace the starter's WHERE 0, which deliberately matches no rows.

Read the supplied fixture before predicting the result. Tiny quiz takes 5 minutes and Word puzzle takes 10, so both pass. Code maze and Logic grid do not pass the combined tests. ORDER BY name puts Tiny quiz before Word puzzle. Keeping the query column as name matters because the check reads that column from answer. A saved table has no inherent display order. Use SELECT name FROM answer ORDER BY name for display; these checks verify membership rather than table scan order.

lesson.title: Aggregate Functions
lesson.summary: Group sessions by subject and calculate counts, totals, and averages.
explanation: An aggregate function combines several values into one result. COUNT counts, SUM adds, and AVG finds the arithmetic average: total divided by the number of known values. GROUP BY makes separate groups before those calculations. A report grouped by subject returns one row for each subject, rather than one row for every session.

Run this complete SQLite example once:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_sessions (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  subject TEXT,
  minutes INTEGER
);
INSERT INTO demo_sessions VALUES
  (1, 'Art', 12),
  (2, 'Art', 24),
  (3, 'Music', 18),
  (4, 'Music', NULL);
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows,
       COUNT(minutes) AS known_minutes
FROM demo_sessions;
```
The result is rows 4 and known_minutes 3. NULL represents an unknown or missing value. It is not zero and is not the text 'NULL'. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(minutes) counts rows with a known minutes value.

A function call puts its input inside parentheses, such as SUM(minutes). AS gives a result column a name, also called an alias. The * in COUNT(*) means count every row; it is not multiplication here. SUM and AVG also ignore NULL inputs. Music's missing duration does not mean a zero-minute session, so it should not pull the known average down.

Run this query after that setup:
```sql
SELECT subject,
       COUNT(minutes) AS session_count,
       SUM(minutes) AS total_minutes,
       AVG(minutes) AS average_minutes
FROM demo_sessions
GROUP BY subject
ORDER BY subject;
```
Art has count 2, total 36, average 18. Music has count 1, total 18, average 18. GROUP BY subject gives each function only the rows for that subject. ORDER BY makes the report's order predictable.

If a group contains only NULL minutes, COUNT(minutes) is 0, while SUM(minutes) and AVG(minutes) are NULL. The average is unknown because there are no known durations to divide by. A grouped query over an empty table returns no groups. A nongrouped COUNT query over an empty table returns 0. Keep these cases distinct instead of inventing a measured zero.

The exercise needs subject and three named calculations: session_count, total_minutes, and average_minutes. Use COUNT(minutes), not COUNT(*), for the requested known-session count. Put all calculations in one SELECT and GROUP BY subject. CREATE TEMP TABLE answer AS saves that grouped result. The starter's numeric zeros are placeholders, not calculated totals.

lesson.title: Joins
lesson.summary: Join two supplied tables and include authors who have no books.
explanation: A join connects related rows from two tables. Each author has one id. A book's author_id points to the id of its author. That relationship lets SQL attach the author's name to each book. Joining does not combine all books into a single text value: one author can appear in several output rows when that author has several books.

AS a and AS b give the tables short names. The dot in a.id means the id column from table a. ON specifies the matching condition: a book belongs to an author when b.author_id equals a.id. REFERENCES documents the relationship in the schema; the ON condition is still needed to tell this query how to join. SQLite enforcement of foreign keys must be enabled separately when you rely on that constraint.

Run this query on the same tables:
```sql
SELECT a.name AS author, b.title
FROM demo_authors AS a
LEFT JOIN demo_books AS b
  ON b.author_id = a.id
ORDER BY a.id, b.title;
```
You get Nora/Garden Gate, Nora/Sea Path, Luis/Sky Notes, and Imani/NULL. LEFT JOIN preserves each left-side author. When there is no matching book, right-side columns are NULL in the result. SQL has not stored an imaginary book for Imani.

The left table matters. Putting books on the left preserves books, not bookless authors. Also, a later WHERE b.title IS NOT NULL removes the unmatched author rows and defeats this goal. Use IS NULL to test missing values; value = NULL does not mean 'is missing' in SQL. COUNT(*) on the joined result counts the unmatched placeholder row too, while COUNT(b.title) counts known titles.

Sets describe distinct members. With A = {red, blue} and B = {blue, green}, blue is the only shared member, so the overlap has size 1. A join is related but can repeat matching rows: it is not automatically a set of distinct names.

On the demo tables above:
```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS joined_rows, COUNT(b.title) AS known_titles
FROM demo_authors AS a
LEFT JOIN demo_books AS b ON b.author_id = a.id;
```
This returns joined_rows=4 and known_titles=3. COUNT receives either * for rows or an expression whose non-NULL values are counted, and returns an integer. It does not change the tables.

The exercise supplies authors and books. Keep authors on the left, join books.author_id to authors.id, and select authors.name AS author with books.title. Save the query in the temporary answer table. The author alias matters because the checks look for that result column. There is no need to remove duplicate author names: repeated names represent distinct books.

Ari Vale has two matches, Bo Lin has one, and Casey North has none. The LEFT JOIN therefore produces four rows, including Casey North with a NULL title. If you got only three rows, check whether you used INNER JOIN or filtered out NULL. If you got too many, check the ON relationship; matching unrelated ids can pair rows incorrectly.

lesson.title: Subqueries
lesson.summary: Find scores above the average for their own subject using a subquery.
explanation: A subquery is a query placed inside another query. It can calculate a number that the outer query uses for comparison. An overall average uses all scores. A group average uses only one subject's scores. For this project, each learner's score must be compared with the average for that same subject.

Run this complete SQLite setup and overall-average query:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_scores (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  learner TEXT,
  subject TEXT,
  score INTEGER
);
INSERT INTO demo_scores VALUES
  (1, 'Nia', 'Art', 50),
  (2, 'Leo', 'Art', 70),
  (3, 'Uma', 'Art', 60),
  (4, 'Nia', 'Music', 100),
  (5, 'Leo', 'Music', 80);
SELECT learner, subject, score
FROM demo_scores
WHERE score > (SELECT AVG(score) FROM demo_scores);
```
The inner query returns the overall average 72. Only the Music scores 100 and 80 exceed it. Parentheses make the inner query a single value used by the outer > comparison.

A correlated subquery refers to the current row of the outer query. Give the outer and inner tables different aliases so the reference is clear. Outer means the row we are deciding about now; inner means rows being averaged. SQL decides results as if it checked each outer row, though the database may optimize how it does the work.

Run the subject-average version on that setup:
```sql
SELECT outer_score.learner,
       outer_score.subject,
       outer_score.score
FROM demo_scores AS outer_score
WHERE outer_score.score > (
  SELECT AVG(inner_score.score)
  FROM demo_scores AS inner_score
  WHERE inner_score.subject = outer_score.subject
);
```
Art's average is 60, so Leo's 70 passes. Music's average is 90, so Nia's 100 passes. Leo's 80 no longer passes. The two aliases keep the inner subject tied to the outer row's subject.

Strictly above means >, not >=. A score equal to its group average is excluded. Be careful with an unqualified column inside a subquery: SQL searches the inner scope first. If both sides refer to the inner table, a condition can compare that row's subject with itself and average all subjects accidentally. Different aliases and fully qualified columns make this mistake visible.

Your answer should contain learner, subject, and score for qualifying rows, saved using CREATE TEMP TABLE answer AS followed by the correlated SELECT. In the corrected exercise fixture, Math has 70, 90, 80, and Dana's 81. Its average is (70 + 90 + 80 + 81) / 4 = 80.25, so Bo's 90 and Dana's 81 pass. Spanish's average remains (95 + 75) / 2 = 85, so Ari's 95 passes. There are three qualifying rows.

An average of no known scores is NULL. A comparison such as score > NULL is unknown and does not pass WHERE. The supplied fixture has known scores in both subjects. To tell whether your query really uses subject averages, try a separate fixture like the walkthrough, where the overall average and group averages choose different rows. Matching one small fixture alone can hide a correlation mistake.

lesson.title: Window functions
lesson.summary: Calculate running totals and ranks within groups using a fixed dataset.
explanation: A window function calculates across related rows while keeping each original row in the result. GROUP BY usually reduces a group to one report row; a window can attach a running total or rank to every practice row. OVER introduces the window's rules: which group to use, which order to follow, and which rows count for a calculation.

Run this complete SQLite setup and running-total query:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_practice (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  subject TEXT,
  day TEXT,
  minutes INTEGER
);
INSERT INTO demo_practice VALUES
  (1, 'Art', '2026-01-01', 10),
  (2, 'Art', '2026-01-02', 25),
  (3, 'Art', '2026-01-03', 25),
  (4, 'Music', '2026-01-01', 8);
SELECT subject, day, minutes,
  SUM(minutes) OVER (
    PARTITION BY subject
    ORDER BY day, id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_total
FROM demo_practice
ORDER BY subject, day, id;
```
Art's totals are 10, 35, 60. Music begins its own total at 8. There are still four output rows.

PARTITION BY subject separates the calculations by subject. ORDER BY day, id inside OVER sets the order for accumulation. Fixed year-month-day text sorts these dates chronologically. id breaks a tie when two sessions share a day. ROWS selects individual rows; UNBOUNDED PRECEDING means the start of the partition, and CURRENT ROW means the row being calculated. SUM adds that whole frame.

Run this ranking query after the same setup:
```sql
SELECT subject, day, minutes,
  RANK() OVER (
    PARTITION BY subject
    ORDER BY minutes DESC
  ) AS duration_rank
FROM demo_practice
ORDER BY subject, day, id;
```
Both Art rows with 25 minutes get rank 1, and the 10-minute row gets rank 3. RANK leaves a gap after a tie because two rows occupy the first two positions. Music's single row ranks 1. Empty parentheses mean RANK needs no direct input argument.

Each window has its own order. Running totals need chronological order; duration ranks need minutes descending, largest first. Do not add id to the ranking order if equal durations should tie: that extra detail would separate them. The outer ORDER BY controls display order, independently of the two window calculations. A rank of 1 does not move that row to the first displayed row by itself.

Mean is another name for the arithmetic average. For 3, 6, 9, add 3 + 6 + 9 = 18, then divide by their count 3: 18 / 3 = 6. A running total stops at each current row; a mean also needs a denominator, so it is a different calculation.

For the exercise, select subject, day, and minutes, then add running_total and duration_rank as named result columns. Save that SELECT as answer. The running-total frame must stop at the current row, rather than sum the entire partition every time. RANK needs PARTITION BY subject so a Spanish session is compared with Spanish sessions.

The supplied Math durations are 20, 30, 30: chronological running totals 20, 50, 80. The two 30-minute entries tie at duration rank 1. Spanish starts again at 15 and then totals 40. The checks now compare every fixture row's running total and rank, including both partitions. They test these results, not every possible input or one required SQL spelling.

lesson.title: Query plans and indexes
lesson.summary: Compare query plans before and after adding an appropriate index.
explanation: An index is an extra structure the database maintains to help it find rows. Think of an index in a book: it can guide you to a topic without reading every page. SQL still decides which rows belong in the result. An index should preserve those intended results; it does not remove duplicates or make every query faster.

Here is a complete small SQLite dataset:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_books (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT,
  genre TEXT
);
INSERT INTO demo_books VALUES
  (1, 'Stone Cities', 'history'),
  (2, 'Cloud Tales', 'fiction'),
  (3, 'Ancient Roads', 'history'),
  (4, 'Trade Routes', 'history');
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT title
FROM demo_books
WHERE genre = 'history'
ORDER BY title
LIMIT 2;
```
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN reports how SQLite plans to find the result; it does not return the titles themselves. The exact plan text can vary. Without a helpful index it may scan rows and use temporary sorting work.

A scan examines many rows. An indexed search can use indexed keys to narrow the search. A composite index has more than one column in a chosen order. An index on genre, title first groups entries by genre, then orders titles within each genre. That fits a query that fixes one genre and sorts by title. LIMIT 2 asks for at most two returned rows.

Run this after the setup:
```sql
CREATE INDEX demo_genre_title
ON demo_books (genre, title);
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT title
FROM demo_books
WHERE genre = 'history'
ORDER BY title
LIMIT 2;
SELECT title
FROM demo_books
WHERE genre = 'history'
ORDER BY title
LIMIT 2;
```
The title result is Ancient Roads, then Stone Cities. The new plan may mention the named index. CREATE INDEX builds it; ON names the table and indexed columns. The query's requested rows remain the same.

An index costs storage and work during INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE because its entries must stay current. SQLite chooses a plan; a tiny table may be fast even without an index. Timing depends on machine load, database size, and caching. Compare identical queries and verify identical results before calling an index helpful. A plan is evidence about strategy, not a guarantee of a particular duration.

A full scan that checks each of n rows once has linear work, written O(n). If a 12-row table needs 12 comparisons, a similar 24-row full scan needs about 24: twice the input gives twice the comparisons. This describes growth of work, not a guaranteed elapsed time. An index may avoid that full scan for a suitable query.

The exercise fixture creates 1,000 books with a recursive number generator. WITH RECURSIVE names an intermediate numbers sequence; UNION ALL appends the next values until value < 1000 becomes false. The || operator joins text, forming titles such as Book 10. The % operator finds the remainder: value % 5 = 0 marks every fifth book history. CASE WHEN chooses history for that condition, otherwise fiction. These are setup mechanics; your task is to add the index and query.

Create the specifically named idx_books_genre_title on books(genre, title), then save the first five history titles in answer with ORDER BY title LIMIT 5. Titles sort as text: Book 100 appears before Book 20. The checks compare the index's key-column metadata and exact selected title membership. Display answer with an explicit ORDER BY title. Inspect the demonstrated EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN before and after; neither these checks nor a particular plan proves a speed gain.
